body:
That's not usually what revocation means in the capability literature sense; revocation is the act of un-granting a capability and all its progeny.  It happens that there is a special case where the thing doing the (un)granting is the heap allocator and we're after heap temporal safety.

If we had a general revocation mechanism, we'd be able to do this for stack allocations as well, and we'd be able to revoke capabilities derived from particular instances of a capability without also revoking all capabilities that pointed to the same piece of memory.  Sadly, no suitable mechanism has yet emerged, and so the only implementations to date are restricted to the case of providing heap temporal safety.

body:
```suggestion
Revocation is the process of clearing the {ctag} of capabilities, and their progeny, that have had their permission to access memory removed.
Enforcing _temporal memory safety_ involves preventing such capabilities from being dereferenced and so prevents use-after-free and use-after-reallocate vulnerabilities.

NOTE: This extension is suitable for _heap temporal safety_ only.

```

body:
I may be off base here, but in the load barrier case, the pointer of the barrier prevent the spread of capabilities that haven't been scanned for possible revocation from an unscanned page to the register file (from where they could spread onward). It doesn't matter if those capabilities are memory capabilities or types, you just need an appropriate bitmap (or other mechanism) to determine if they should be revoked and a mechanism to do so.

In CheriBSD we don't currently revoke type capabilities (e.g., on Morello), but we do revoke both heap capabilities allocated by malloc and capabilities previously returned by mmap where the whole reservation has been unmapped. Similar ideas can be used to handle tokens, type capabilities, etc.

body:
Svucrg is "just" a way of letting privileged software front-run capability fetches from memory.  It's a mechanism that might be useful to software.  (ETA2: It isn't a _necessary_ mechanism nor is it a _sufficient_ one.  It just seems to be a nice to have, simple enough in hardware and a performance boost to software.  Software implementing Reloaded-style global revocation has to do a lot of other work in addition to the MMU maintenance around Svucrg.)  It _happens_ that CHERIvoke/Cornucopia/Reloaded-style "global revocation" -- the special case where we can use capability monotonicity in lieu of a materialized capability provenance tree -- is particularly straightforward to implement atop this: front-run every capability load (either by Svucrg traps or by just getting to the page first in the background scan) and for each capability in the system, check some flat global state (the revocation bitmap).  (ETA: please note that "particularly straightforward" is still some 80 pages of technical report and some thousands of lines of code spanning the CheriBSD kernel and user space.)  The same approach works for sealing rights as address space, as there's nothing that ties the "flat global state" to "address space" other than software, so it's easy to have -- and in fact the CheriBSD implementation has stubs for -- a "sealing-type revocation bitmap" next to your "address-space revocation bitmap".  (By contrast, (CHERI+)MTE more tightly couples the flat global state with address space, by virtue of storing colors at (physical; please let's not talk about vMTE) memory locations.)

_In principle_ software could be maintaining more elaborate state -- something more hierarchical and less flat -- so that a capability found at a given location in memory could be associated with (a subsequence of) its provenance, enabling the front-running privileged software to discriminate between Alice's copies of (progeny of) a capability and Bob's copies of (progeny of) the same capability.  We don't know how to do that efficiently or securely, especially not in the case of adversarial (arbitrary) instructions (in contrast to, say, CHERI's monotonicity properties).

All of that to say, I think the text for Svucrg should much more stick to what it does, mention in a note that it is intended to enable privileged software to front-run capability loads, cite the Reloaded paper ("which may be useful for software wishing to provide certain forms of temporal safety [387]"), and be done with it.  IMHO, there's no need to explain revocation in this text.

body:
It would be a spec change - but I think this state should be defined to say "Clear loaded tag".
The rationale is to be able to control access to the capabilities on a page, and so declare CRW=0, CD=1 to mean "there are caps here but you can't see them"

The case which came up was when a whole page of memory has been freed, and CD is set then it becomes possible to prevent access to it and retain the information that it actually does include capabilities. This could be used to clear the tags via the tag controller, for example, without needing to zero the memory.

It's what the logical meaning of CRW=0, CD=1 would mean anyway.

Perhaps the main advantage of allowing this state is for Svadu hardware setting of PTE.CD.
If one core sets CRW=0, then another core cannot legally set PTE.CD on the same page without risking an invalid PTE end result, unless it doesn't an atomic CAS on the PTE bits in memory (i.e. only update if it finds that CRW=1)

see https://github.com/riscv/riscv-cheri/issues/920

body:
I hate to continue to be a pest, but... can this _please_ be more carefully worded?

1. It's still on supervisory software to implement revocation; this extension is _just_ providing some useful architectural traps.
2. It's not the general "capability revocation" that capability-systems people mean, so some qualification of the term is ideal.
3. CHERIvoke/Cornucopia/Reloaded has never attempted to prevent UAF, _just_ UAR.  (CHERIoT's load barrier closes the UAF/UAR gap, trapping on the earlier UAF, and CHERI+MTE makes the gap significantly less meaningful but does not completely _close_ it in its mismatching-stores-fizzle mode.)

Perhaps something like...

"When enabled, the extension adds the ability for supervisory software to quickly front-run loads of capabilities from userspace pages.  Such a facility has been shown to be a useful primitive for system-level implementation of certain forms of capability revocation which, in turn, allow userspace heap allocator software to deterministically guard against use-after-reallocation cite:[cornucopia-reloaded]."

-=== Enabling Software or Hardware PTE updates
+NOTE: Because the state of _pte.cd=1_ and _pte.crw=0_ is illegal, it is possible for the update of _pte.cd_ to fail if another thread has cleared _pte.crw_.
 
-The decision about whether to take exceptions on capability stores with the {ctag} set to a page with PTE.CRW=1 and PTE.CD=0 is determined by whether the _Svade_ and _Svadu_ extensions are enabled.
-These cause PTE Accessed and Dirty updates to be done in software, via the exception handler, or by a hardware mechanism respectively.
+NOTE: Capability dirty tracking _always_ checks the {ctag} on stored capabilities, it is not optional as the value of the {ctag} is always available to the microarchitecture.
body:
That's been a point of contention.  In speculative execution, the AGU result for a store instruction may be ready significantly before the datum to be stored is.  Historically, for at least memory-like regions of the address space, there's been no need to hold the store instruction itself in speculation after the AGU result and translation thereof have completed, but this makes translation's trapping behavior dependent on the data as well.

An open research question is whether some one-sided error here is tolerable, especially in combination with `Svadu` (cap-dirtying a cap-capdirtyable page even if it turns out that the cap-sized datum in fact had a clear tag bit).

body:
This is certainly true - however the stored tag (along with the rest of the store data) must be known before the commit point of the store - i.e. before the point where the determination is made whether to raise the exception.

This is not true for loads on any CPU I've ever worked on - the exception detection is always done before the load data is known. RISC-V does offer load data triggers, so such a thing is in the architecture, but it's optional fortuantely.

So I think the split here is sensible.

body: I agree that the split is sensible, but, just to emphasize the point I was trying to make: in earlier systems, it's generally _not_ required that you know _what_ you're storing, just _where_ you're storing it, before you can be certain not to trap on that store.  That is, the store _instruction_ can speculatively retire (is that the right phrase? speculatively commit?), promising to not trap, if the store buffer is able to hold an as-yet-unknown value at a (speculatively) known address.  That is, while program-order-earlier instructions may yet still be unresolved (and may yet trap!) -- in particular, the ones computing the value to be stored -- if the AGU and TLB have signed off, the store _instruction_ is done and it might be cheaper to track its uncommitted effects in the store buffer than in the general instruction speculation state.
